J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. In this appeal, the appellant M/s Adani Power (formerly known as
Adani Power Maharashtra Limited) has assailed the order dated 10.12.2020
passed by 1st respondent Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission
(hereinafter referred to as “the Commission” or “MERC”) passed in
Miscellaneous Application No.54/2020 in Case nos.290/2018.
2. The appellant is a generating company and owns as well as operates
a generating station of capacity 3300MW (660X5) at Tiroda in the State of
Maharashtra. It has entered into following four Power Purchase Agreements
(PPAs) with the 2nd respondent Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution
Company Limited (in short MSEDCL) which is a distribution licensee in the
State of Maharashtra: -
(i) PPA dated 08.09.2008 for 1320MW;
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 2 of 21

(ii) PPA dated 31.03.2010 for 1200MW;
(iii) PPA dated 09.08.2010 for 125MW; and
(iv) PPA dated 16.02.2013 for 440MW.
3. The appellant had approached the Commission with the petition
bearing no.290/2018 seeking compensation on account of Change in Law
events occasioned by the changes in the coal supply assurance contained
in the New Coal Distribution Policy, 2007 (“NCDP 2007”) and related matters.
4. The said petition bearing no.290/2019 was disposed of by the
Commission vide order dated 07.02.2019 thereby approving shortfall in
domestic coal allocation under SHAKTI Policy as a Change in Law event and
directed that methodology for computation of compensation shall be the
same as approved in its order dated 07.03.2018 in case nos.189/2013 and
140/2014 for coal shortfall on account of amendment of NCDP 2007.
5. Aggrieved by the order of the Commission dated 07.02.2019 passed
in petition no.290/2018, the appellant filed appeal no.155/2019 before this
Tribunal on the grounds of the operational parameters of SHR & GCV,
quantum of shortfall and on the directions of the Commission for prior
intimation of estimated energy charge. MSEDCL also challenged the said
order vide appeal no.116/2019 on the grounds that SHAKTI Policy does not
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 3 of 21

constitute Change in Law and no Carrying Cost is admissible on any Change
in Law relief de hors the PPAs.
6. Following reliefs were sought by the appellant in its appeal
no.155/2019: -
“(a) Hold and declare that the impact of Change in Law
shall not be linked to the net SHR as submitted in the Bid
and instead the impact of Change in Law would be
considered on the basis of SHR as per MERC MYT
Regulations, 2011, whichever is lower, and modify
paragraphs 23 and 24 of the Impugned Order accordingly;
(b) Hold and declare that the impact of Change in Law for
domestic coal supply should not be computed considering
the middle value of GCV range of assured coal grade and
instead the impact of Change in Law would be considered
on the basis of as received/actual GCV of coal, and modify
paragraphs 23 and 24 of the Impugned Order accordingly;
(c) Hold and declare that the Appellant shall be entitled to
Change in Law compensation for actual shortfall in supply
of domestic coal by CIL and its subsidiaries in accordance
with the revised Tariff Policy, 2016 vis-à-vis the quantity
of coal assured under the NCDP 2007; and
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 4 of 21

(d) Hold and declare that the existing methodology of
MOD stack of providing energy charge details should be
made applicable for the Appellant's generating station
irrespective of various fuel source used within the same
generating station and modify paragraph 26 accordingly.
(e) Pass such further orders or directions as this Hon'ble
Tribunal may deem just and proper in the circumstances
of the case.”
7. Both these appeals i.e. appeal nos.155/2019 and 116/2019 were
disposed of by this Tribunal vide common judgment dated 28.09.2020
thereby setting aside the Commission’s order dated 07.02.2019 and allowing
the claims of the appellant in appeal no.155/2019. The relevant portion of
the judgment as well as its operative part/final order is extracted
hereinbelow: -
“15.1 Issue No.1:-We hold that the introduction of
SHAKTI POLICY amounts to change in law and all the
ingredients of change in law are duly met under the
respective PPAs. The impugned order is therefore
affirmed on this issue.
15.2 Issue No.2:- We hold that findings in the impugned
order relating to the issue of restricting the quantum of
shortfall in domestic coal to a maximum of 25% are
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 5 of 21

against the basic principles of restitution under the change
in law provisions of the PPAs.
15.3 Issue No.3:- In line with our judgment dated
14.09.2020 in Appeal No.182 of 2019, we hold that the
change in law compensation shall be calculated based on
the SHR specified in the MERC MYT Regulations, 2011
or the actual SHR whichever is lower and actual GCV of
coal as received as the plant site.
……….
16. In view of the above, the Appeal No. 155 of 2019
deserves to be allowed and Appeal No. 116 of 2019 is
liable to be dismissed.
ORDER
For the foregoing reasons, we are of the considered view
that the issues raised in the Appeal No. 155 of 2019 have
merits and hence, appeal is allowed. The Appeal No.116
of 2019 is dismissed as devoid of merits.
The impugned order dated 07.02.2019 passed by
Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission in Case
No. 290 of 2018 is hereby set aside to the extent decided
in our findings, stated supra.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 6 of 21

The State Commission is directed to issue the
consequential orders as expeditiously as possible within
a period of three months from the pronouncement of this
judgment / order.”
(Emphasis supplied)
8. Manifestly, upon holding the introduction of SHAKTI Policy to be a
Change in Law event and reversing the finding of the Commission related to
issue of restricting the quantum of shortfall in domestic coal to the maximum
of 25% and further holding that the Change in Law compensation shall be
calculated based on the SHR specified in the MERC MYT Regulations, 2011
or the actual SHR whichever is lower and actual GCV of coal as received on
the plant site, this Tribunal finally directed the Commission to issue
consequential orders in this regard as expeditiously as possible.
9. Thereafter, the appellant approached the Commission by way of
Miscellaneous Application bearing no.54/2020 seeking consequential reliefs
in terms of the above noted judgment of this Tribunal. The application has
been disposed of by the Commission vide order dated 10.12.2020 which has
been impugned in the instant appeal.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 7 of 21

10. Perusal of the impugned order of the Commission would reveal that
the Commission has conducted a fresh full-fledged hearing on the following
issues framed by it for its consideration: -
“a. Whether SHR as specified in MYT Regulations 2011 is
to be used or SHR specified in MYT Regulations notified
from time to time be used for relevant period?
b. Whether as received GCV is to be used as such or ceiling
on degradation in GCV needs to be provided?
c. Whether coal shortfall is to be computed with reference to
actual receipt of the coal or coal offered by Coal companies
which was not fully lifted by petitioner?
d. Whether advance intimation of cost of fuel is to be given
to Discoms?
e. Whether compensation on account of coal supply is to be
limited to normative generation?
f. What is modified methodology for computing Change in
Law compensation?”
11. On issue no.(a), the Commission has ruled SHR stipulated in MYT
Regulations applicable for that relevant period shall be used as reference
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 8 of 21

SHR. However, FY 2016-17 shall be exception for this rule and as directed
in Order dated 7 March 2018, SHR as stipulated in MYT Regulations 2011
(and not MYT Regulations 2015) shall be used as reference for FY 2016-17.
Actual SHR or reference SHR as stipulated in applicable MYT Regulations,
whichever is lower shall be used for computation of Change in Law
compensation.
12. On issue no.(b), the Commission ruled that its ruling given in MA
No.53/2020 is squarely applicable in this case and held that (a) Actual SHR
or reference SHR as stipulated in applicable MYT Regulations, whichever is
lower shall be used for computation of Change in Law compensation. (b)
For the period governed by MYT Regulations, 2015, as received GCV shall
be considered for computing Change in Law compensation on account of
coal shortfall. And for period of 1 April, 2020 onwards, as received GCV with
ceiling limit as allowed in MYT Regulations 2019 needs to be considered for
computation of Change in Law compensation. (c) Formula agreed by APML
and MSEDCL, and approved by the Commission in MA No 53 of 2020 for
arriving at as received GCV of coal for circumstances when no actual coal
has been received under MoU shall be used in present matter also. (d) Also,
APML shall pass on credit notes, incentive or compensation received from
coal companies to MSEDCL.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 9 of 21

13. On issue no.(c), the Commission has ruled that APML shall be entitled
for Change in Law compensation towards actual shortfall in domestic coal
supply as assured under SHAKTI Policy.
14. On issue no.(d), the Commission has ruled that although as directed
by the APTEL, APML is not required to give advance intimation of estimated
energy charge due to alternate coal supply, APML needs to comply with
provisions of State Grid Code Regulations 2020 notified on 2 September,
2020 relating to seeking approval of Change in Law impact at the earliest
(not later than one month) and include such impact in MoD stack.
15. On issue no.(e), the Commission has ruled that any generation above
the normative PLF on annual basis would not be eligible for any
compensation on account of coal shortfall.
16. On issue no.(f), the Commission has given the tables containing the
formulae for computing Change in Law compensation.
17. Accordingly, the Commission has modified its order dated 07.02.2019
and has formulated a methodology for computation of Change in Law
compensation allowed by it vide previous order dated 07.02.2019.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 10 of 21

18. Following three grounds have been urged before us on behalf of the
appellant in assailing the said impugned order dated 10.12.2020 of the
Commission: -
(i) The Commission has committed an error in directing
application of SHR specified in MERC MYT Regulations
notified from time to time instead of SHR specified in the
MERC MYT Regulations, 2011 or actual SHR achieved by
the appellant, as held by this Tribunal in judgment dated
28.09.2020;
(ii) The Commission has committed an error in directing a
ceiling on “as received GCV” of coal for the period
01.04.2020 onwards despite this Tribunal having directed
application of “as received GCV” at the plant site without any
ceiling for calculation of Change in Law compensation for the
relevant period; and
(iii) The Commission has also erred in restricting the Change in
Law compensation to coal required for normative
generation/PLF relying on its own order dated 28.11.2020 in
case no.132/2020 which was passed subsequent to the
judgment dated 28.09.2020 of this Tribunal as the same is
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 11 of 21

contrary to the said judgment of this Tribunal in which
complete restitution was allowed to the appellant without any
limitation or ceiling on the quantum of coal shortfall.
19. We have heard Mr. Amit Kapur, learned counsel appearing for the
appellant, Mr. Ramji Srinivasan, learned senior counsel appearing for the 1st
respondent Commission and Mr. B.P. Patil, learned senior counsel
appearing for the 2nd respondent MSEDCL.
20. In the light of rival submissions made by the learned counsels/senior
counsels on behalf of the parties, the issue which arises for our consideration
in this appeal is as to whether the Commission has traversed beyond the
directions issued by this Tribunal in the judgment dated 28.09.2020 in appeal
no.155/2019, whereby the case was remanded to the Commission with the
directions to issue consequential orders.
21. Rules 23 and 23A of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, govern the
powers of an appellate court to remand a case back to the court/forum from
whose decree/order the appeal was preferred. Rule 23 provides that where
the trial court has decided a suit and passed a decree only on a “preliminary
issue” without recording any findings on the other issues and subsequently
on appeal, the appellate court reverses the decree, the appellate court may
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 12 of 21

remand the case back to the trial court so as to render decision on the other
issues as well which were not decided previously. Rule 23A was inserted in
Order 41 through amending Act of the year 1976. This rule enables the
appellate court to remand a case even when the trial court or the lower court
has decided all the issues on merits other than on the basis of a preliminary
point only. Thus, Rule 23A has widened the scope of the powers of appellate
court in remanding a case. This Provision empowers the appellate court to
remand a case back to the trial court for fresh consideration or
reconsideration wherever considered necessary. The phrase used therein
is “considered necessary”. While there can be no fixed criteria as to when it
would be considered necessary to remand a case back to the trial court, it
has been left to the discretion of the appellate court.
22. The remand orders passed by appellate court can be of various types:-
(a) Where the original decree/order of the lower court is completely set
aside and the case is remanded back for fresh consideration, the
lower court has the power to reopen the entire case, rehear the
arguments and pass a completely fresh judgment.
(b) Where the appellate court keeps the appeal pending before it and
remands only a particular issue to the lower court for fresh hearing,
the lower court has only the limited power to try only that specific
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 13 of 21

issue and return its findings back to the appellate court without
passing a fresh judgment.
(c) Where the appellate court remands the matter exclusively for
passing consequential order, the power of the lower court becomes
more specific, mechanical and restrictive. In that case, the lower
court cannot rehear the arguments or re-examine the facts or alter
the substantive findings already given by the appellate court. The
powers of the lower court would be strictly limited to passing orders
that naturally and logically flow from the decision given by the
appellate court.
23. We may note that when an appellate court remands a case back to
lower court, the powers of lower court are strictly bound and limited by the
specific directions, scope and purpose mentioned in the remand order. The
lower court cannot go beyond the specific instructions/directions given by the
appellate court and cannot reopen the entire case unless expressly
permitted by the appellate court. Lower court cannot re-adjudicate the issues
that the appellate court has already answered.
24. In the instant case, we have already noted hereinabove that this
Tribunal had, in the judgment dated 28.09.2020 given its findings upon
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 14 of 21

various issues raised by the appellants in the batch of appeals on the
following issues: -
Issue No. 1:- Whether introduction of SHAKTI Policy does not
amount to Change in Law under the PPAs entered into between
APML and MSEDCL and whether APML has not provided notice
of such Change in Law to the Respondent MSEDCL.
Issue No. 2:- Whether the MERC is correct in holding that for the
purpose of Change in Law compensation, shortfall in domestic
coal shall be limited to a maximum of 25% of ACQ after the
introduction of SHAKTI Policy?
Issue No. 3:- (a) Whether the MERC was correct in holding that
the net SHR submitted by the Appellant in its bid or SHR and
Auxiliary Consumption norms specified for new generating
stations under the MYT Regulations, 2011, whichever is superior
shall form the basis for computing Change in Law compensation
under the PPAS?
(b) Whether the MERC was correct in holding that the reference
GCV of domestic coal supplied by CIL shall be the middle value
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 15 of 21

of GCV range of assured coal grade in LoA/FSA/MoU and not
the GCV as received?
Issue No.4:- Whether the MERC was justified in directing APML
to provide advance intimation of impact on energy charge by
using alternate coal for the purpose of Merit Order purchase?
Issue No.5:- Whether the Respondent MSEDCL is justified in
contesting APML's entitlement to Carrying Cost.
25. The above issues were summarized and answered by this Tribunal in
the said judgment as under: -
“15.1 Issue No.1:-We hold that the introduction of
SHAKTI POLICY amounts to change in law and all the
ingredients of change in law are duly met under the
respective PPAs. The impugned order is therefore
affirmed on this issue.
15.2 Issue No.2:- We hold that findings in the impugned
order relating to the issue of restricting the quantum of
shortfall in domestic coal to a maximum of 25% are
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 16 of 21

against the basic principles of restitution under the change
in law provisions of the PPAs.
15.3 Issue No.3:- In line with our judgment dated
14.09.2020 in Appeal No.182 of 2019, we hold that the
change in law compensation shall be calculated based on
the SHR specified in the MERC MYT Regulations, 2011
or the actual SHR whichever is lower and actual GCV of
coal as received as the plant site.
15.4 Issue No.4:- We find that the directions issued by the
State Commission regarding advance intimation
requirement is not consistent with normal Rules of MOD
preparation and also does not provide a level playing field
for IPPs.
15.5 Issue No.5:- We find that allowance of carrying cost
is a settled position of law and the State Commission has
already allowed the same to the Appellant, APML.”
26. The final order of this Tribunal in the said judgment is very material and
is reproduced hereinbelow: -
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 17 of 21

“ORDER
For the foregoing reasons, we are of the considered view
that the issues raised in the Appeal No. 155 of 2019 have
merits and hence, appeal is allowed. The Appeal No.116
of 2019 is dismissed as devoid of merits.
The impugned order dated 07.02.2019 passed by
Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission in Case
No. 290 of 2018 is hereby set aside to the extent decided
in our findings, stated supra.
The State Commission is directed to issue the
consequential orders as expeditiously as possible within
a period of three months from the pronouncement of this
judgment / order.
In view of the disposal of the Appeal, the relief sought in
the IA No.505 of 2019 in Appeal No. 116 of 2019 does not
survive for consideration and accordingly,stands disposed
of.
No order as to costs.”
(Emphasis supplied)
27. We may note that issue “whether compensation on account of coal
supply is to be limited to normative generation” as framed by the Commission
in the impugned order upon which findings have been returned against the
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 18 of 21

appellant, was never raised before this Tribunal during the hearing of the
appeal no.155/2019 which was allowed vide judgment dated 28.09.2020.
Therefore, the Commission ought not to have either framed such issue for
its consideration or proceeded to give its findings on the same for the simple
reason that no such issue was remanded to the Commission for
consideration/fresh decision by this Tribunal vide judgment dated
28.09.2020.
28. Further, it is crystal clear that upon giving its findings on the issues
raised by the appellant in the appeal, this Tribunal directed the Commission
to issue consequential orders in the light of findings returned on these issues
in the said judgment. Therefore, it was not a case where this Tribunal had
remanded the case back to the Commission for fresh hearing/fresh
consideration and for passing a fresh order. The remand was very specific
and limited i.e. just to pass consequential orders in terms of the decision
rendered by this Tribunal in the said judgment. What the Commission was
required to do was only to make computations with regards to the benefits to
which the appellant was entitled on account of the Change in Law events as
decided and allowed by this Tribunal in the said judgment dated 28.09.2020.
On the contrary, what the Commission has done is that it has reopened the
case altogether and has conducted the hearing afresh on all the issues,
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 19 of 21

which had already been decided by this Tribunal and has passed a fresh
order which runs contrary to the said judgment dated 28.09.2020 of this
Tribunal.
29. It is inexplicable to us as to how the Commission ventured beyond the
remit of this Tribunal in conducting a fresh hearing of the case and returning
findings contrary to what has been decided by this Tribunal. The
Commission was only required to pass consequential orders in terms of the
findings returned on the issues by this Tribunal in the said judgment and
ought not to have conducted a fresh hearing thereby violating the judicial
discipline. The conduct of the Commission in doing so is not only deplorable
and reprehensible but also contemptuous in nature. The Commission has
totally disobeyed and disregarded the directions issued by this Tribunal in
the judgment dated 28.09.2020 not only by reopening the entire case and
conducting a fresh hearing but also by contradicting the decision of this
Tribunal and returning findings which are absolutely contrary to those
rendered by this Tribunal. In our considered opinion, the Commission has
committed contempt of this Tribunal. However, we refrain from initiating any
contempt proceedings against the Commission in the hope that the
Commission would adhere to the judicial discipline and would comply with
the judgments/orders/directions of this Tribunal in letter and spirit in future.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.317 of 2021 Page 20 of 21

30. In view of above discussion, the impugned order of the Commission
cannot be sustained. The same is hereby set aside. The Commission is
again directed to issue consequential orders in favour of the appellant in the
light of the judgment of this Tribunal dated 28.09.2020 in appeal no.155/2019
within a period of six weeks from the date of receipt of this judgment
positively.
31. The appeal as well as pending applications, if any, stand disposed of
accordingly.
Pronounced in the open court on this the 19th day of August, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson
REPORTABLE / NON-REPORTABLE

J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. In this appeal, the appellant M/s Adani Power (formerly known as
Adani Power Maharashtra Limited) has assailed the order dated 10.12.2020
passed by 1st respondent Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission
(hereinafter referred to as “the Commission” or “MERC”) passed in
Miscellaneous Application No.53/2020 in Case nos.189/2013 and 140/2014.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 2 of 20

2. The appellant is a generating company and owns as well as operates
a generating station of capacity 3300MW (660X5) at Tiroda in the State of
Maharashtra. It has entered into following four Power Purchase Agreements
(PPAs) with the 2nd respondent Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution
Company Limited (in short MSEDCL) which is a distribution licensee in the
State of Maharashtra: -
(i) PPA dated 08.09.2008 for 1320MW;
(ii) PPA dated 31.03.2010 for 1200MW;
(iii) PPA dated 09.08.2010 for 125MW; and
(iv) PPA dated 16.02.2013 for 440MW.
3. The appellant had approached the Commission with the petition
bearing no.189/2013 seeking compensation on account of Change in Law
events occasioned by the changes in the coal supply assurance contained
in the New Coal Distribution Policy, 2007 (“NCDP 2007”) and related matters.
4. The said petition was disposed of by the Commission vide order dated
15.07.2014 thereby approving a framework for determination of
compensatory fuel charge considering the decision dated 21.06.2013 of the
Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) and the advice dated
31.07.2013 issued by the Ministry of Power, Govt. of India to all the Electricity
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 3 of 20

Regulatory Commissions. In compliance of the said order dated 15.07.2014,
the appellant filed another petition bearing case no.140/2014 praying therein,
inter alia, for approving a mechanism for determination of compensatory tariff
and to recognize the CCEA decision, NCDP amendment of 2013 and advice
dated 31.07.2013 issued by Ministry of Power, Govt. of India as Change in
Law events as per the provisions of the Power Purchase Agreements. Vide
order dated 20.08.2014 passed in the said petition, the Commission
formulated a mechanism for passthrough of compensatory fuel charges that
had been allowed in case no.189/2013. The review petition filed by the
appellant against the said order dated 20.08.2014 was dismissed by the
Commission.
5. Two separate appeals bearing appeal nos.129/2016 and 130/2016
were filed by the appellant before this Tribunal against the orders dated
15.07.2014 and 20.08.2014 passed by the Commission in petition
nos.189/2013 and 140/2014 respectively. The 2nd respondent MSEDCL also
filed cross appeals against these two orders of the Commission vide appeal
nos.187/2016 and 188/2016.
6. All these appeals were disposed of by this Tribunal vide judgment
dated 04.05.2017 thereby remanding all the issues raised by the parties in
these appeals to the Commission for fresh consideration in the light of
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 4 of 20

judgment dated 11.04.2017 passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Civil
Appeal Nos.5399-5400 of 2016 titled Energy Watchdog v. CERC and Ors.
7. The Commission passed a fresh order dated 07.03.2018 in case
no.189/2013 and 140/2014 wherein it allowed the claims of the appellant on
account of changes in the NCDP 2007 as Change in Law under Article 13 of
the PPA dated 08.09.2008 and Article 10 of the remaining three PPAs
executed between the parties but at the same time restricted the relief of
Change in Law for 1180MW capacity to the extent of minimum supply
obligations specified for the CIL subsidiaries in the last four years of the 12th
Five Year Plan period i.e. FY 2013-14 to FY 2016-17 as per the NCDP 2013.
The Commission also held that the alternate coal quantity for meeting the
domestic coal shortfall shall be computed on the basis of Station Heat Rate
(SHR) mentioned by the appellant in the bid documents and the middle value
of Gross Calorific Value (GCV) range of assured coal grade for domestic
coal as per the FSA/LoA/MoU.
8. The said order dated 07.03.2018 of the Commission was assailed by
the appellant before this Tribunal by way of appeal no.182/2019. Following
reliefs were sought by the appellant in the said appeal: -
“(a) Hold and declare that the impact of Change in Law
shall not be linked to the net SHR as submitted in the Bid
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 5 of 20

and instead the impact of Change in Law would be
considered on the basis of SHR as per MERC MYT
Regulations, 2011, or actual, whichever is lower, and
modify paragraphs 91 and 92 of the Impugned Order
accordingly;
(b) Hold and declare that the impact of Change in Law for
domestic coal supply should not be computed considering
the middle value of GCV range of assured coal grade and
instead the impact of Change in Law would be considered
on the basis of as received/ actual GCV of coal, and
modify paragraphs 91 and 92 of the Impugned Order
accordingly;
(c) Hold and declare that the Appellant shall be entitled to
Change in Law compensation for actual shortfall in supply
of domestic coal by CIL and its subsidiaries in accordance
with the revised Tariff Policy, 2016 vis-à-vis the quantity
of coal assured under the NCDP 2007; and
(d) Pass such further orders or directions as this Tribunal
may deem just and proper in the circumstances of the
case.”
9. The appeal was disposed of by this Tribunal vide judgment dated
14.09.2020 thereby setting aside the Commission’s order dated 07.03.2018
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 6 of 20

and allowing the claims of the appellant. The relevant portion of the
judgment as well as its operative part/final order is extracted hereinbelow: -
SHR for Change in Law compensation -
“7.14 From the aforesaid discussion, it emerges that this
Tribunal has already held that the SHR submitted in the
bid (when it is not a bid parameter as per the bidding
guidelines) by a generating company is not to be used as
the basis for computing the coal shortfall requirement and
thereby for computation of change in law compensation to
be awarded to the generating company. Such linking of
change in law compensation to the SHR mentioned in the
bid documents would not restitute the affected party to the
same economic position as if the approved change in law
event had not occurred. This issue is therefore decided in
favour of the Appellant and the Respondent No. 2 is
directed to allow change in law compensation on the basis
of the SHR specified in the MERC MYT Regulations, 2011
or the actual SHR achieved by the Appellant, whichever
is lower. This would sufficiently protect the interests of the
consumers against any plant inefficiency being passed on
to the Discoms or the consumers.”
GCV for Change in Law compensation –
“8.9 For the aforesaid reasons, this issue is decided in
favour of the Appellant and it is directed that the
compensation for the Change in Law approved by the
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 7 of 20

MERC shall be computed on the basis of actual GCV of
coal received.
Compensation for actual shortfall in coal
9.12 From the above decision, it is clear that the
methodology for compensation in case of shortfall in
domestic coal under the NCDP regime cannot be different
from the methodology for compensation in case of
shortfall under the SHAKTI Policy. This Tribunal has
already held that the shortfall in domestic coal supply
needs to be measured against 100% supply assurance
contained under the NCDP 2007 and when measured
against this assurance, restricting Change in law relief to
the maximum of 35% to 25% for the respective four years
of the 12th plan is not justified. This issue is, therefore,
decided in favour of the Appellant and the Impugned
Order is set aside to the extent it limits the Change in Law
relief to the Appellant with reference to the maximum of
(1) actual quantum of coal offered for offtake by CIL, and
(2) the minimum assured quantum as per the NCDP 2013
for the respective year. We direct that the Respondent
MSEDCL shall compute Change in Law compensation on
the basis of actual shortfall in supply of domestic coal
suffered by the Appellant from the start date approved by
the MERC.
………….
ORDER
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 8 of 20

For the foregoing reasons, we are of the considered view
that the issues raised in the instant Appeal No. 182 of
2019 have merits and hence, appeal is allowed.
The impugned order dated 07.03.2018 passed by
Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission in Case
Nos. 189 of 2013 and 140 of 2014 are hereby set aside to
the extent challenged in the Appeal and our findings,
stated supra.
The State Commission is directed to issue the
consequential orders as expeditiously as possible within
a period of three months from the pronouncement of this
judgment / order.”
(Emphasis supplied)
10. Manifestly, upon holding that impact of Change in Law shall be
considered on the basis of SHR specified in the MERC MYT Regulations,
2011 or actual SHR achieved by the appellant, whichever is lower and
directing that the compensation for Change in Law with regards to domestic
coal supply to be computed on the basis of actual GCV of coal received as
well as actual shortfall in supply of domestic coal suffered by the appellant,
this Tribunal finally directed the Commission to issue consequential orders
in this regard as expeditiously as possible.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 9 of 20

11. In pursuance to these directions of this Tribunal, the appellant
approached the Commission with an application bearing Miscellaneous
Application No.53/2020 in the month of October, 2020 seeking consequential
relief. The application has been disposed of by the Commission vide order
dated 10.12.2020 which has been impugned in the instant appeal.
12. Perusal of the impugned order of the Commission would reveal that
the Commission has conducted a fresh full-fledged hearing on the following
issues framed by it for its consideration: -
“a. Whether SHR as specified in MYT Regulations 2011 is
to be used or SHR specified in MYT Regulations notified
from time to time is to be used for relevant period?
b. Whether as received GCV is to be used as such or ceiling
on degradation in GCV needs to be provided?
c. Whether coal shortfall is to be computed with reference to
actual receipt of the coal or coal offered by Coal companies
which was not fully lifted by petitioner?
d. Whether compensation on account of coal supply is to be
limited to normative generation?
e. What is the modified methodology for computing Change
in Law compensation?”
13. On issue no.(a), the Commission has ruled that SHR stipulated in MYT
Regulations applicable for the relevant period shall be used as reference
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 10 of 20

SHR. However, FY 2016-17 shall be exception for this rule and as directed
in Order dated 7 March, 2018, SHR as stipulated in MYT Regulations 2011
(and not MYT Regulations 2015) shall be used as reference for FY 2016-17.
Actual SHR or reference SHR as stipulated in applicable MYT Regulations,
whichever is lower shall be used for computation of Change in Law
compensation.
14. On issue no.(b), the Commission has held that in MYT Regulations
2019 which has been made applicable from 1 April ,2020 onwards, the
Commission has limited the difference between as billed GCV and as
received GCV to 300 kCal/kg. Therefore, for period of 1 April, 2020 onwards,
as received GCV with ceiling limit as allowed in MYT Regulations 2019 would
need to be considered for computation of Change in Law compensation. In
the opinion of the Commission this dispensation is also consistent with
APTEL judgment which clearly recorded APML’s readiness to use parameter
which is beneficial to consumer.
15. On issue no.(c), the Commission has ruled that the appellant shall be
entitled for change in law compensation towards actual shortfall in domestic
coal supply as assured under NCDP 2007.
16. On issue no.(d), the Commission has ruled that any generation above
the normative Plant Load Factor (PLF) on annual basis would not be eligible
for any compensation on account of coal shortfall.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 11 of 20

17. On issue no.(e), the Commission has given the tables containing the
formulae for computing Change in Law compensation.
18. Accordingly, the Commission has modified its order dated 07.03.2018
and has formulated a methodology for computation of Change in Law
compensation allowed by it vide previous order dated 07.03.2018.
19. Following two grounds have been urged before us on behalf of the
appellant in assailing the said impugned order dated 10.12.2020 of the
Commission: -
(i) The Commission has committed an error in directing
application of SHR as specified in MERC MYT Regulations
notified from time to time instead of SHR specified in the
MERC MYT Regulations, 2011, which was specified by this
Tribunal in the judgment dated 14.09.2020 in appeal
no.182/2019;
(ii) The Commission has committed an error in directing a
ceiling on “as received GCV” of coal for the period
01.04.2020 onwards when this Tribunal had directed
application of “as received GCV” without any ceiling for
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 12 of 20

calculation of Change in Law compensation for the relevant
period.
(iii) The Commission has also erred in restricting the Change in
Law compensation to coal required for normative
generation/PLF.
20. We have heard Mr. Amit Kapur, learned counsel appearing for the
appellant, Mr. Ramji Srinivasan, learned senior counsel appearing for the 1st
respondent Commission and Mr. B.P. Patil, learned senior counsel
appearing for the 2nd respondent MSEDCL.
21. In the light of rival submissions made by the learned counsels/senior
counsels on behalf of the parties, the issue which arises for our consideration
in this appeal is as to whether the Commission has traversed beyond the
directions issued by this Tribunal in the judgment dated 14.09.2020 in appeal
no.182/2019, whereby the case was remanded to the Commission with the
directions to issue consequential orders.
22. Rules 23 and 23A of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, govern the
powers of an appellate court to remand a case back to the court/forum from
whose decree/order the appeal was preferred. Rule 23 provides that where
the trial court has decided a suit and passed a decree only on a “preliminary
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 13 of 20

issue” without recording any findings on the other issues and subsequently
on appeal, the appellate court reverses the decree, the appellate court may
remand the case back to the trial court so as to render decision on the other
issues as well which were not decided previously. Rule 23A was inserted in
Order 41 through amending Act of the year 1976. This rule enables the
appellate court to remand a case even when the trial court or the lower court
has decided all the issues on merits other than on the basis of a preliminary
point only. Thus, Rule 23A has widened the scope of the powers of appellate
court in remanding a case. This Provision empowers the appellate court to
remand a case back to the trial court for fresh consideration or
reconsideration wherever considered necessary. The phrase used therein
is “considered necessary”. While there can be no fixed criteria as to when it
would be considered necessary to remand a case back to the trial court, it
has been left to the discretion of the appellate court.
23. The remand orders passed by appellate court can be of various types:-
(a) Where the original decree/order of the lower court is completely set
aside and the case is remanded back for fresh consideration, the
lower court has the power to reopen the entire case, rehear the
arguments and pass a completely fresh judgment.
(b) Where the appellate court keeps the appeal pending before it and
remands only a particular issue to the lower court for fresh hearing,
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 14 of 20

the lower court has only the limited power to try only that specific
issue and return its findings back to the appellate court without
passing a fresh judgment.
(c) Where the appellate court remands the matter exclusively for
passing consequential order, the power of the lower court becomes
more specific, mechanical and restrictive. In that case, the lower
court cannot rehear the arguments or re-examine the facts or alter
the substantive findings already given by the appellate court. The
powers of the lower court would be strictly limited to passing orders
that naturally and logically flow from the decision given by the
appellate court.
24. We may note that when an appellate court remands a case back to
lower court, the powers of lower court are strictly bound and limited by the
specific directions, scope and purpose mentioned in the remand order. The
lower court cannot go beyond the specific instructions/directions given by the
appellate court and cannot reopen the entire case unless expressly
permitted by the appellate court. Lower court cannot re-adjudicate the issues
that the appellate court has already answered.
25. In the instant case, we have already noted hereinabove that this
Tribunal had, in the judgment dated 14.09.2020 given its findings upon
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 15 of 20

various issues raised by the appellant particularly on the following three
issues: -
(i) Whether the Commission was correct in holding that the net
SHR submitted by appellant in its bid or SHR and auxiliary
consumption norms specified for new generating stations
under the MYT Regulations, 2011, whichever is superior,
shall form the basis for computing Change in Law
compensation under the PPAs? and
(ii) Whether the Commission was correct in holding that the
reference GCV of domestic coal supplied by CIL shall be the
middle value of GCV range of assured coal grade in
LoA/FAS/MoU and in the GCV as received?
(iii) Whether the Commission was correct in restricting Change
in Law compensation to coal required for normative
generation/PLF?
26. The issue with regards to the SHR was answered by this Tribunal in
the said judgment as under: -
“This issue is therefore decided in favour of the Appellant
and the Respondent No. 2 is directed to allow change in
law compensation on the basis of the SHR specified in the
MERC MYT Regulations, 2011 or the actual SHR
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 16 of 20

achieved by the Appellant, whichever is lower. This would
sufficiently protect the interests of the consumers against
any plant inefficiency being passed on to the Discoms or
the consumers.”
27. The issue with regards to GCV was answered by this Tribunal in the
said judgment as under: -
“For the foregoing reasons, the issue is decided in favour
of the appellant and it is directed that the compensation
for Change in Law approved by the MERC shall be
computed on the basis of actual GCV of coal received.”
28. The issue with regards to limiting of Change in Law compensation to
normative generation was answered by this Tribunal in the said judgment as
under: -
“We direct that the Respondent MSEDCL shall compute
Change in Law compensation on the basis of actual
shortfall in supply of domestic coal suffered by the
Appellant from the start date approved by the MERC.”
29. The final order of this Tribunal in the said judgment is very material and
is reproduced hereinbelow: -
“ORDER
For the foregoing reasons, we are of the considered view
that the issues raised in the instant Appeal No. 182 of
2019 have merits and hence, appeal is allowed.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 17 of 20

The impugned order dated 07.03.2018 passed by
Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission in Case
Nos. 189 of 2013 and 140 of 2014 are hereby set aside to
the extent challenged in the Appeal and our findings,
stated supra.
The State Commission is directed to issue the
consequential orders as expeditiously as possible within
a period of three months from the pronouncement of this
judgment / order.
No order as to costs.
(Emphasis supplied)
30. It is crystal clear that upon giving its findings on the three issues raised
by the appellant in the appeal, this Tribunal directed the Commission to issue
consequential orders in the light of findings returned on these issues in the
said judgment. Therefore, it was not a case where this Tribunal had
remanded the case back to the Commission for fresh hearing/fresh
consideration and for passing a fresh order. The remand was very specific
and limited i.e. just to pass consequential orders in terms of the decision
rendered by this Tribunal in the said judgment. What the Commission was
required to do was only to make computations with regards to the benefits to
which the appellant was entitled on account of the Change in Law events as
decided and allowed by this Tribunal in the said judgment dated 14.09.2020.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 18 of 20

On the contrary, what the Commission has done is that it has reopened the
case altogether and has conducted the hearing afresh on all the issues,
which had already been decided by this Tribunal and has passed a fresh
order which runs contrary to the said judgment dated 14.09.2020 of this
Tribunal.
31. It is inexplicable to us as to how the Commission ventured beyond the
remit of this Tribunal in conducting a fresh hearing of the case and returning
findings contrary to what has been decided by this Tribunal. The
Commission was only required to pass consequential orders in terms of the
findings returned on the issues by this Tribunal in the said judgment and
ought not to have conducted a fresh hearing thereby violating the judicial
discipline. The conduct of the Commission in doing so is not only deplorable
and reprehensible but also contemptuous in nature. The Commission has
totally disobeyed and disregarded the directions issued by this Tribunal in
the judgment dated 14.09.2020 not only by reopening the entire case and
conducting a fresh hearing but also by contradicting the decision of this
Tribunal and returning findings which are absolutely contrary to those
rendered by this Tribunal. In our considered opinion, the Commission has
committed contempt of this Tribunal. However, we refrain from initiating any
contempt proceedings against the Commission in the hope that the
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.316 of 2021 Page 19 of 20

Commission would adhere to the judicial discipline and would comply with
the judgments/orders/directions of this Tribunal in letter and spirit in future.
32. In view of above discussion, the impugned order of the Commission
cannot be sustained. The same is hereby set aside. The Commission is
again directed to issue consequential orders in favour of the appellant in the
light of the judgment of this Tribunal dated 14.09.2020 in appeal no.182/2019
within a period of six weeks from the date of receipt of this judgment
positively.
33. The appeal as well as pending applications, if any, stand disposed of
accordingly.
Pronounced in the open court on this the 19th day of August, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson

IN THE APPELLATE TRIBUNAL FOR ELECTRICITY

Counsel for the Appellant(s) : Mukul Rohatgi, Sr. Adv.
K. Parmeshwar, Sr. Adv.
Vishal Biond
Abhikalp Pratap Singh
Siddharth Dharmadhikari

O R D E R
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. In this order we will be considering the request of the appellant seeking
withdrawal of this appeal with liberty to file a review petition before the
Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as
“the Commission”) and with further liberty to approach this Tribunal again
subject to the outcome of the review proceedings.
2. The appellant Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company
Limited (in short “MSEDCL”) has filed the instant appeal against the common
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.11 of 2026 Page 2 of 17

order dated 24.12.2025 passed by the Commission in case number
233/2024 (filed by the appellant) and case number 218/2025 (filed by 2nd
respondent JSW Energy Limited). The appellant had in case number
233/2024 challenged certain invoices raised by the 2nd respondent for the
period 01.11.2022 to 30.06.2025 in terms of the Power Purchase Agreement
(PPA) dated 23.02.2010 executed between the parties, whereas the 2nd
respondent had in case number 218/2025 sought enforcement of the terms
of the said PPA dated 23.02.2010.
3. Vide the impugned order, the Commission dismissed the petition filed
by the appellant and allowed the petition filed by the 2nd respondent thereby
directing the appellant to pay approximately Rs.568/- crores to 2nd
respondent towards differential energy charges along with Rs.31.17 crores
towards fixed charges as well as the late payment surcharge.
4. We may note that the Ministry of Power, Government of India issued
directions under Section 11 of the Electricity Act, 2003 on 05.05.2022
directing all the imported coal based generating stations including the
Ratnagiri unit of 2nd respondent to operate at full installed capacity. These
directions remain in force from 05.05.2022 to 31.12.2022 and from
16.03.2023 to 30.06.2025. The thermal power plant of 2nd respondent
located at Ratnagiri was specifically named and included in these directions
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.11 of 2026 Page 3 of 17

issued by the Ministry of Power from time to time. In the impugned order
dated 24.12.2025, the Commission held that these directions issued by the
Ministry of Power are not applicable to the Unit-1 of 2nd respondent as it is
an intrastate generating station falling under the jurisdiction of Government
of Maharashtra for the reason that "appropriate government" for an intrastate
station is the State Government and not the Central Government. Based on
such finding and observing that since Section 11 Benchmark ECR later on
became lower than the PPA tariff, the Commission held 2nd respondent
eligible for differential energy charges and accordingly passed directions as
noted hereinabove.
5. Along with the appeal, the appellant has filed application bearing IA
No.17/2026 seeking interim relief in the nature of stay of the operation of the
common order dated 24.12.2025 passed by the Commission. This
application was heard by us on 18.03.2026. Upon hearing the learner senior
counsel for the appellant on that date, we did not feel inclined to pass any
interim order as sought by the appellant, and accordingly, dismissed the
application. The said order dated 18.03.2026 was assailed by the appellant
before the Hon'ble Supreme Court by way of Civil Appeal No.4682/2026
which was disposed of vide order dated 30.04.2026 with the directions to this
Tribunal to rehear the interim application of the appellant and dispose of the
same vide a reasoned order in accordance with law.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.11 of 2026 Page 4 of 17

6. Accordingly, we took up the interim application bearing IA No.17/2026
again for hearing on 18.05.2026.
7. On the subsequent date i.e. 20.05.2026, we heard the learned senior
counsel for the appellant, Mr. Mukul Rohatgi, learned Solicitor General, Mr.
Tushar Mehta, for the 1st respondent i.e. the Commission and learned senior
counsel, Dr. A.M. Singhvi, appearing for 2nd respondent. Learned Solicitor
General made a very unusual and unconventional submission that the
Commission is willing to reconsider the impugned order upon his advice that
the impugned order may not stand judicial scrutiny in this appeal, and
therefore, urged us to set aside the impugned order and to remand the case
back to the Commission for fresh consideration. However, the learned senior
counsel for the 2nd respondent objected to these submissions of the learned
solicitor general saying that the 2nd respondent was successful before the
Commission and therefore, its rights would be seriously prejudiced in case
the impugned order is set aside and remanded to the Commission for a fresh
consideration without a proper hearing.
8. Accordingly, we heard the learned senior counsels appearing on behalf
of the appellant and 2nd respondent as well as the learned Solicitor General
appearing on behalf of the 1st respondent Commission on 15.07.2006 and
27.07.2026 in detail on this aspect.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.11 of 2026 Page 5 of 17

9. We may note that on 27.07.2026 Mr. Mukul Rohatgi, learned senior
counsel appearing for the appellant submitted that the appellant wishes to
withdraw the appeal and hence, the same may be dismissed as withdrawn
with liberty to the appellant to approach the Commission with a petition for
review of the impugned order. This submission on behalf of the appellant
was vehemently objected to by Dr. Abhishek Manu Singhvi and Mr. Sanjay
Sen, learned senior counsels appearing on behalf of the 2nd respondent. Mr.
Tushar Mehta, learned solicitor general reiterated that the impugned order
of the Commission needs reconsideration by the Commission and the case
may either be remanded back to the Commission for fresh consideration or
the appellant may be permitted to withdraw the appeal with liberty, as sought
by the appellant.
10. In so far as the prayer on behalf of the appellant seeking permission to
withdraw the appeal is concerned, there cannot be any opposition to the
same as it is for the appellant to decide whether or not to pursue the appeal
before this Tribunal. The only issue which arises for our consideration is
whether or not to grant liberty to the appellant for approaching the
Commission with a petition for review of the impugned order dated
24.12.2025.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.11 of 2026 Page 6 of 17

11. Learned senior counsel for the appellant would argue that the
impugned order of the Commission is without jurisdiction in so far as the
Commission has exercised power akin to judicial review which are
unavailable to it under the Electricity Act, 2003 by holding that the direction
under Section 11 of the Electricity Act issued by Ministry of Power are
inapplicable to intrastate unit of 2nd respondent, and therefore, appellant
ought to be granted liberty to invoke the review jurisdiction of the
Commission so that the error apparent on the face of record in the impugned
order dated 24.12.2025 is rectified. He submitted that withdrawal of appeal
with liberty to institute review proceedings before the Commission is a
recognized practice before this Tribunal and the on this aspect referred to
the order dated 31.10.2023 passed in appeal no.518/2023 (KSEB v. KERC
& Ors. and order dated 19.02.2018 passed in appeal no.147/2017 PGCIL v.
CERC & Ors. He urged us to allow the prayer of the appellant for withdrawal
of the instant appeal with liberty to approach the Commission by way of the
review petition and with further liberty to approach this Tribunal again subject
to final outcome of the proposed review proceedings.
12. On behalf of 2nd respondent, it was submitted by the learned senior
counsels Dr. Singhvi and Mr. Sen that this is an unprecedented case of an
adjudicator appearing through a law officer saying that its own order is
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.11 of 2026 Page 7 of 17

wrong, which is unheard of. It is submitted that an adjudicator taking sides
with a litigant before itself makes mockery of the objectivity and
independence between the stakeholders and the regulators. According to
the learned senior counsels, this is an attempt to de-facto have the appeal
allowed without adjudication while derailing the proceedings on remand
before this Tribunal. On this aspect, reference is made to Airports Economic
Regulatory Authority of India v. Delhi International Airport Ltd, 2024(15) SCC
345.
13. It is further argued that an adjudicator like Electricity Regulatory
Commission cannot take a stand contrary to its judgment. Reliance, in this
regard, is placed on Opto Circuit India Ltd. v. Axis Bank, 2021 (6) SCC 707.
It is argued that since in the instant case, substantive and vested rights have
come into existence in favour of 2nd respondent by way of the impugned
order of the Commission, the appellant has no right to withdraw the appeal
with liberty to file a review petition. The learned counsels pointed out that
the impugned order of the Commission has even been partially complied with
by the appellant and permission to withdraw the appeal with liberty, as
sought, at this juncture will destroy the substantive and vested right of the
2nd respondent. It is also submitted that granting such liberty at this stage,
when the appellant seriously prosecuted the appeal as well as the interim
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.11 of 2026 Page 8 of 17

application before this Tribunal as well as before Hon'ble Supreme Court,
would be contrary to the provisions of Section 114 and Order 47 Rule 1 of
Civil Procedure Code, and if permitted, such course would encourage forum
shopping.
Our Analysis:
14. While the statutory appellate tribunals like this Tribunal are not strictly
bound by the technicalities of the Code of Civil Procedure, however, by virtue
of Section 120 of the Electricity Act, 2003, this Tribunal is required to take
guidance from the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and for various
provisions it is vested with same powers as are vested in a Civil Court under
the Code of Civil Procedure. Normally, this Tribunal has been applying the
underlying principles of justice, equity and fair play as envisaged under the
Code of Civil Procedure.
15. Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure which relates to the appeals
from original decrees and provides the procedure to be followed by an
appellate court in dealing with such appeals, does not have any provision for
withdrawal of the appeals, with or without liberty, as sought by the appellant.
Therefore, we have to fall back on Order 23 of the Code of Civil Procedure
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.11 of 2026 Page 9 of 17

which relates to withdrawal of suits or abandonment of part of a claim by the
plaintiff. We find it apposite to extract the said legal provision hereunder:
“1. Withdrawal of suit or abandonment of part of claim.—
(1) At any time after the institution of a suit, the plaintiff
may as against all or any of the defendants abandon his
suit or abandon a part of his claim: Provided that where
the plaintiff is a minor or other person to whom the
provisions contained in rules 1 to 14 of Order XXXII
extend, neither the suit nor any part of the claim shall be
abandoned without the leave of the Court.
………….
(3) Where the Court is satisfied,—
(a) that a suit must fail by reason of some formal defect,
or
(b) that there are sufficient grounds for allowing the
plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the subject matter of suit
or part of a claim,
It may, on such terms as it thinks fit grant the plaintiff
permission to withdraw from such suit or such part of the
____________________________________________________________________________________

claim with liberty to institute a fresh suit in respect of the
subject-matter of such suit or such part of the claim.
………….. ”
16. While Rule 1(1) of Order 23 does not create any bar upon a
plaintiff/appellant from withdrawing the suit/appeal against all or any of the
defendants/respondents, Rule 1(3) envisages that the court may grant the
plaintiff/appellant permission to withdraw suit/appeal with liberty to institute
fresh proceedings in respect of the subject matter of such suit/appeal only if
the court is satisfied that: -
(a) the suit/appeal must fail by reason of some formal defect; or
(b) that there are sufficient grounds for allowing the plaintiff/appellant
to institute a fresh suit for the subject matter of the suit/appeal or
part of a decree.
17. Therefore, as already noted hereinabove, the appellant is free to
withdraw its appeal at any time. No fetters can be placed upon such right
of the appellant as appellant is the master of its case and can chose whether
or not to prosecute the appeal.
18. The request of the appellant herein for withdrawal of the instant appeal
has, thus, to be allowed. However, the question arises whether the liberty,
as sought by the appellant, can be granted to it.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.11 of 2026 Page 11 of 17

19. We may note that permission to reserve liberty is not an absolute right.
Such an order must reflect the court’s satisfaction that sufficient and valid
legal grounds justifying grant of liberty existed. Courts or tribunals do not
grant liberty as a matter of routine. An appellant, seeking liberty, must show
a formal defect in the appeal or other sufficient grounds for either
approaching a more appropriate statutory authority or the lower court/forum,
which has passed impugned order, with a review petition.
20. In the case at hand, it is not the case of the appellant that the appeal
suffers from any formal defect. The appellant is seeking liberty to approach
the Commission with a petition for review of the impugned order.
21. The case of the appellant, as supported by the Commission itself, is
that the impugned order of the Commission is palpably erroneous and
therefore, deserves to be reviewed by the Commission. The Commission,
through learned Solicitor General, also contends that the impugned order
may not stand legal scrutiny by the Tribunal and hence, it is willing to
reconsider the same.
22. We feel intrigued by these contentions agitated on behalf of the
appellant and echoed by the Commission. By filing the instant statutory
appeal under Section 111 of the Electricity Act, 2003 the appellant
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.11 of 2026 Page 12 of 17

consciously chose its remedy against the “erroneous” order of the
Commission. In case, the impugned order is erroneous which would not
withstand the legal scrutiny by this Tribunal, there was no reason or occasion
for the appellant to seek withdrawal of the appeal with liberty to approach the
Commission again with a petition for review of the impugned order. The
appellant ought to have prosecuted the appeal on merit and demonstrated
before this Tribunal that the impugned order is not legally sustainable. Upon
being satisfied, this Tribunal would have allowed the appeal and set aside
the impugned order. The conduct of the appellant in seeking liberty to file a
review petition before the Commission instead of prosecuting the appeal
before this Tribunal indicates the attempt of forum shopping by the appellant
which can not be permitted.
23. Further, it is to be noted that according to the appellant, the impugned
order of the Commission is without jurisdiction and according to the
Commission, the impugned order would not stand the legal scrutiny in this
Tribunal. Evidently, neither the appellant nor the Commission states that the
impugned order suffers any “error apparent on the face of record” warranting
review under Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC. Therefore, it is not understandable
as to what had made the appellant to withdraw this statutory appeal and seek
review of the impugned order before the Commission. Moreover, by filing
the instant appeal before this Tribunal, the appellant chose its remedy
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.11 of 2026 Page 13 of 17

against the impugned order and effectively waived off its right to seek a
review before the Commission itself. Thus, granting liberty to revert to review
proceedings before the Commission now would circumvent the statutory
restriction and permit forum shopping.
24. The conduct of the appellant post filing of the appeal also deserves
consideration. Right since the filing of the appeal, the appellant has been
prosecuting it vehemently and pressing its prayer for interim relief. Vide
order dated 18.03.2026, we dismissed the application for interim relief. The
appellant assailed the said order in the Hon'ble Supreme Court by way of
Civil Appeal No.4682/2026 which was disposed of vide order dated
30.04.2026 directing this Tribunal to rehear the parties on the interim
application and dispose of the same by a reasoned order in accordance with
law. Accordingly, arguments on the interim application were heard on
20.05.2026 and 15.07.2026 during which the learned senior counsel
appearing for the appellant made strenuous effort to make out a case for
grant of interim order in favour of the appellant. However, towards the
conclusion of his arguments on 15.07.2026, learned senior counsel for the
appellant sought to withdraw the appeal with liberty to approach the
Commission again with a review petition. This prayer was reiterated by the
learned senior counsel on 27.07.2026. Such sudden change of heart on the
part of the appellant is not understandable. It gives an impression that the
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.11 of 2026 Page 14 of 17

appellant has probably realized lack of merit in its appeal and thus wants to
have a second bite at cherry by approaching the Commission with a review
petition. Seeking withdrawal of an appeal simply because the appellant
realizes that its case before the appellate court is weak does not constitute
either a “formal defect” or “sufficient cause” envisaged under Sub-Rule 3 of
Rule 1 of Order 23 CPC.
25. We cannot also lose sight of the fact that the impugned order of the
Commission, which is also stated to have been partially complied with by the
appellant, has created a vested right in favour of the 2nd respondent. More
importantly, the Hon'ble Supreme Court also while passing the order dated
30.04.2026 in appellant’s Civil Appeal No.4682/2026, has directed the
appellant to pay a sum of Rs.250 crores to the 2nd respondent as an interim
measure. Therefore, allowing the appellant to withdraw the appeal with
liberty to approach the Commission again with a review petition, would nullify
the rights created in favour of the 2nd respondent by the impugned order of
the Commission as well as by the above noted order dated 30.04.2026 of
the Hon'ble Supreme Court and would force the 2nd respondent to relitigate
the entire matter from the scratch before the Commission thereby causing it
severe financial as well as procedural prejudice which is impermissible in
law.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.11 of 2026 Page 15 of 17

26. In Rakesh Bhatia & Ors. v. Pramod Sharma & Ors. 2009 (112) DRJ
143, the Hon'ble Delhi High Court has very clearly held that if the appellate
court feels that the appellant had at an initial stage only of the appeal opted
or agreed to apply for review, the appellate court would grant such liberty but
if the time of the appellate court has been taken in attempting to persuade
the court in admitting the appeal or to issue the notice thereafter and only
after availing to do so withdrawal is sought, the appellate court may decline
to grant such liberty to apply for review. In the instant case, not only has the
appellant vigorously pursued the appeal and made strenuous attempts to
persuade this Tribunal to pass interim order in its favour but also approached
the Hon'ble Supreme Court when this Tribunal declined to pass interim
orders in its favour and dismissed the interim application. The appellant not
only consumed the time of this Tribunal on various dates, as noted
hereinabove, in arguing the application for interim relief but also consumed
the time of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No.4682/2026.
Therefore, viewed from this angle also, this is not a fit case where liberty
ought to be granted to the appellant to file a review petition before the
Commission.
27. In so far as the submission of learned Solicitor General to the effect
that the Commission is willing to reconsider the impugned order as, upon his
advice, the same would not stand scrutiny by this Tribunal, is concerned we
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.11 of 2026 Page 16 of 17

note that apart from making such oral submission the learned Solicitor
General did not make any attempt to take us through the impugned order to
demonstrate why the same appears to him to be erroneous and would not
stand scrutiny by this Tribunal. We are afraid that we cannot set aside an
order of the Commission and remand the case back to the Commission for
reconsideration merely on the asking of the Commission without gaining
satisfaction that such submission is made bonafide and upon sound legal
basis. Since no such endeavour has been made on behalf of the
Commission to explain the infirmity in the impugned order which would
require reconsideration by the Commission, apart from the bald oral
submissions made by learned Solicitor General, we are unable to
countenance these submissions of the learned Solicitor General.
28. Considering the above discussion, request of the appellant for liberty
to approach the Commission by way of a review petition is hereby declined.
29. The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn. All pending applications also
stand disposed of accordingly.
